newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech CSOB to appeal ministry takeover of OBI.
newsitem.headline: Czech CSOB to appeal ministry takeover of OBI.

text.p: Ceskoslovenska Obchodni Banka a.s. (CSOB) said on Wednesday that the finance ministry's takeover of its investment unit, OB Invest, was unnecessary and the bank would appeal the decision.

"We expect that (OB Invest) will submit its appeal in the legally allowed period because... there were no legal reasons for the forced administration," said a statement from CSOB's spokesman Milan Tomanek.
The Finance Ministry said on Tuesday that its securities oversight bureau would impose forced administration on OB Invest (OBI) from Wednesday because of repeated violations of financial laws.
The ministry said the violations were in connection with OB Invest's management of the investment funds Zlaty Investicni Fond Kvanto a.s., and Kvanto Investicni Privatizacni Fond a.s..
The move was the strongest action yet taken against an investment arm of one the country's four largest banks.
The government said earlier this year it would begin cracking down on financial crime after years of widespread criticism about insider trading and opaque practices.

The ministry said regulators had found "profound and repeated violations of the law" and called the move "preventative...to limit the further possibility of damaging the interests or property of investors".

It said the violations were connected to buying shares to create majority stakes in unspecified firms at an "overvalued price" and then selling stakes at an "undervalued price", and conducting operations "having a character of forbidden lending which does not hold to lawfully permitted limits".
The ministry did not elaborate and officials have declined further comment. OBI has 15 days to appeal but it is still unclear how any appeal might be handled.
The ministry appointed Petr Kraus as OB Invest's administrator from its list of authorised officials.

Tomanek said, without elaborating, that the reason for the ministry's action had occurred more than half a year ago and that the firm had already made a "marked personnel exchange" and a "marked change in policy" in response.

"We are convinced that this strongest form that the finance ministry chose to fix the shortfalls found at (OBI) was avoidable," he said, adding that CSOB had been cooperating with the authorities and OBI had been taking the steps demanded.

Tomanek said CSOB had been building "chinese walls" to separate the bank from investment activities of its other units and would guarantee its further cooperation with authorities to make amends for "all which is confirmed as an actual violation of laws or ethical practice connected with OBI".

CSOB praised steps the ministry had been taking in its recent attempts to bring more transparency to the beleaguered Czech markets. But it took issue with the ministry announcing its action to the media without telling OBI.
"We are surprised with the form in which the forced administration was published without the concurrent announcement of such a serious fact to our investment company," Tomanek added.
